word:hebrew:H103.explanation: Agar means to harvest or gather.

word:hebrew:H1034.explanation: Beth is a Hebrew proper name used for a place. It is not presented here as a general action, quality, or object word, but as the name of a location. This name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both within Joshua 19:6. The available rendering preserves the name as “Beth,” so its precise significance as a place name depends on the surrounding verse and geographic context.

word:hebrew:H1081.explanation: Baladan is the name of a Babylonian prince.

word:hebrew:H1126.explanation: Ben-Oni is the original name of Benjamin.

word:hebrew:H1232.explanation: Bukkiah is a Hebrew personal name. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or idea. In the Old Testament, this name appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 25, and the English rendering is consistently “Bukkiah.” The name’s precise significance is not defined by the available lexical information, so it is best understood here as the personal name of the individual identified in those genealogical and service records.

word:hebrew:H1311.explanation: This Hebrew word expresses “all,” referring to the whole of a group, amount, or set rather than only part of it. It functions as a concise term of completeness or totality. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Exodus 12:9 and Numbers 6:19. Its exact role in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning points to something viewed in its entirety.

word:hebrew:H1368.explanation: Gibbôwr means powerful or mighty. It can also describe a warrior or champion, including mighty men of valor.

word:hebrew:H1496.explanation: Gazith means cut or dressed stone.

word:hebrew:H1539.explanation: Geled means skin, specifically human skin.

word:hebrew:H1575.explanation: Gammad means a warrior, one who grasps weapons. The Gammadims are shown in towers, hanging shields on the walls.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: The primary claim that gaph means “the back” cites W1, but W1 supports only the “himself” rendering and does not directly support the stated sense. Thus the primary claim fails the required lexical-plus-Scripture evidence standard.

word:hebrew:H176.explanation: Ow means “or,” presenting alternatives. It can also mean “if,” introducing a condition.

word:hebrew:H1764.explanation: It refers to “millet,” the name of a particular cultivated grain. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Ezekiel 4:9. There it functions as the name of an item included among things prepared and given, rather than describing a person, action, or quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning is millet.

word:hebrew:H1908.explanation: Hadad is a personal name, rendered “Hadad” in English. It identifies named people in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs 12 times across 11 verses, appearing in Genesis, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Its surrounding scriptural associations include named figures, kingship, and death, but those events belong to the individuals who bear the name, not to the meaning of the name itself.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: The explanation uses the secondary gloss “shew/showing” while its primary lexical definition is “respect, i.e. partiality.” LEX_DEF is attached but does not support the stated sense, so the primary claim is lexically mismatched.

word:hebrew:H2031.explanation: This Hebrew word means “thoughts,” referring to what a person holds in the mind. It describes inward mental activity rather than an outward action or physical object. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 4:5, so its normal meaning is known from this single occurrence and its consistent English rendering. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but the central idea remains thoughts formed or experienced within the mind.

word:hebrew:H2048.explanation: Hâthal means to mock or deride. It can also mean to deceive or deal deceitfully.

word:hebrew:H208.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Onam,” identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, and each occurrence is rendered “Onam.” The name occurs in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, including several family-record passages. Its meaning here is therefore primarily nominative: it distinguishes a particular individual in Israel’s recorded lineage rather than describing that person’s character or role.

word:hebrew:H2084.explanation: This Hebrew word means “gain.” It identifies gain as the idea being expressed in a sentence, rather than naming a person, place, or action. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 2:8. The word’s basic meaning remains focused and limited: gain. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical idea itself is clear.

word:hebrew:H2105.explanation: Zoheth is a personal name, rendered “Zoheth” in English. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:20. Because no explicit definition or broader usage is available, its lexical meaning cannot be stated more precisely from this evidence. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage, but the word itself functions as a name.

policy.futureRepairGate: Reopen only after a verified source-alignment, lexical-identity, or evidence-view correction materially changes the closed evidence.
policy.priorReviewerNotes: The explanation elevates the secondary “vilest” gloss while omitting the supplied primary lexical definition, “a shaking, perhaps a tempest.” Scripture supports the observed rendering, but does not establish it as the word’s primary meaning.

word:hebrew:H2295.explanation: Hoglah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Hoglah.” It identifies one individual in Israel rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, appearing in Numbers and Joshua. Its repeated use across these passages confirms that it functions as a proper name. The available material does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the name’s underlying meaning, so it is best understood simply as the personal name Hoglah.

word:hebrew:H2462.explanation: Helbah is a proper name, rendered “Helbah,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Judges 1:31, so its meaning is chiefly its identity as the named place or entity in that passage. The surrounding lexical relationships connect it with verbs for dwelling and driving out, but the verse text is needed to explain the specific statement.

word:hebrew:H2480.explanation: Chalat means to snatch at or catch.

word:hebrew:H2567.explanation: This Hebrew word can mean “fifth” or “take.” It appears once in the Old Testament, at Genesis 41:34, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. The surrounding verse determines whether it functions as a number-related term or as an action word. Its recorded role there is as the sentence’s predicate, expressing what is proposed or carried out. The word therefore points either to the fifth part or to taking, depending on the immediate wording.

word:hebrew:H2589.explanation: Channôwth means supplication, an appeal asking for gracious treatment.

word:hebrew:H2633.explanation: Chōsen means wealth, riches, or treasure.

word:hebrew:H271.explanation: Ahaz is a personal name. It is used for a king of Judah and for a man listed among Micah’s sons.

word:hebrew:H2714.explanation: Cheqer means examination or searching out—the act of looking into something to find what is there. It can also refer to counting or number, and to deliberation, such as searching of the heart.

word:hebrew:H2813.explanation: “Hashabniah” is a personal name, identifying a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Nehemiah: 3:10 and 9:5. As a name, its meaning in a sentence is primarily identifying: it tells the reader who is being mentioned. The surrounding verse is needed to determine that person’s specific role in each passage.

word:hebrew:H2866.explanation: Chăthath means dismay or casting down.

word:hebrew:H2938.explanation: Ta'am means to taste. It can also mean to perceive figuratively, as in “taste and see” that Yahweh is good.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: Ezra 6:14 directly supports a commandment/decree sense, but it does not directly support the claim that the word means a judicial sentence. The single claim therefore does not satisfy the required exact Scripture support.

word:hebrew:H3050.explanation: Yah is the sacred name for Yahweh.

word:hebrew:H312.explanation: Acher means other or another, referring to a person or thing distinct from one already mentioned. It can also mean following, as when one group comes after another.

word:hebrew:H3124.explanation: Jonah is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H3191.explanation: This Hebrew verb means “seem.” It functions as a verb, expressing a speaker’s assessment of how something is regarded rather than naming a person, object, or action. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 7:18. Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, the precise force of the word in that sentence must be understood from the passage around it.

word:hebrew:H3317.explanation: Yiphtah-el is a Hebrew name used in the Old Testament, not a common word with an available descriptive definition. It occurs four times, all within Joshua 19, and is associated with two references in that chapter: Joshua 19:14 and Joshua 19:27. Its repeated use in this territorial section indicates that it identifies a named location. The precise significance of the name itself cannot be stated from the available lexical information, but its normal function here is as a place designation.

word:hebrew:H3418.explanation: Yereq means green vegetation or grass.

word:hebrew:H3461.explanation: This Hebrew word is a personal name rendered as “Ishmerai.” It identifies one individual in the Old Testament and does not provide an ordinary descriptive meaning in the available lexical information. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:18, within a genealogical record. Because it functions as a name, its importance is identifying the person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The surrounding verse and family record provide the context for understanding its place there.

word:hebrew:H3586.explanation: This Hebrew word means “lying,” referring to speech or conduct that is untrue. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its ordinary lexical sense is clearest from this rendering rather than from a broad range of uses. The word occurs in Isaiah 30:9, and its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. It functions as a description of lying, identifying what is characterized by untruth rather than naming a person or place.

word:hebrew:H3616.explanation: Kâleh means pining—failing with longing as one looks for someone.

word:hebrew:H3663.explanation: Kenanjah is the name of an Israelite, rendered Chenaniah in English.

word:hebrew:H3722.explanation: Kaphar means to cover, including covering with pitch. It can also describe making atonement before Yahweh, with forgiveness following.

word:hebrew:H3883.explanation: This Hebrew word means “winding.” It describes something that turns or follows a curving course rather than proceeding straight. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Kings 6:8. Its basic sense identifies the shape or direction of something as winding, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what object is being described. It should therefore be understood as a descriptive word for a curved or turning course, not as a broader spiritual or symbolic term by itself.

word:hebrew:H3977.explanation: This word refers to “balances,” the instrument used to weigh or compare the value of something. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 5:27, so its normal meaning is supported by a single usage rather than a broad range of passages. The word names the weighing device itself; the surrounding verse is needed to explain how that image functions in Daniel’s message.

word:hebrew:H3999.explanation: Mabbûwl means a deluge or flood.

word:hebrew:H4118.explanation: Mahêr means hurrying or being in a hurry, expressed as doing something quickly.

word:hebrew:H4161.explanation: Motsa means a going forth, an exit, or something that comes out. It describes words proceeding from lips and horses brought out from Egypt.

word:hebrew:H4222.explanation: Machah means to clap or strike the hands together.

word:hebrew:H4363.explanation: Mikmas is the name of a place in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H442.explanation: This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Alush.” It identifies a named place or station rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers 33:13–14. Since no explicit definition is preserved, its meaning is limited to the name itself: Alush, a location named in Israel’s wilderness journey. Its precise significance beyond that name is not given here.

word:hebrew:H4424.explanation: Melatjah is the name of a Gibeonite.

word:hebrew:H4491.explanation: “Driving” refers to the act or manner of driving, describing how movement is directed. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs twice, both in 2 Kings 9:20, and both English renderings present it as “driving.” It functions as a descriptive word within the sentence, identifying the driving being observed or reported. Its exact force in the verse depends on the surrounding wording.

word:hebrew:H4550.explanation: Massa means a departure or journey. It describes Israel moving forward on its journeys from the wilderness of Sinai.

word:hebrew:H4617.explanation: Maʻăneh means a reply or answer, whether favorable or contradictory.

word:hebrew:H4859.explanation: Mashshahah means a loan. It can also refer to a debt.

word:hebrew:H4936.explanation: “Misham” is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew text, this name appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 8:12, and the available rendering preserves it as “Misham.” Because no short definition or descriptive gloss is provided, the name itself is the supported meaning: it distinguishes this person from others in the genealogy. Its specific family connection belongs to the surrounding verse and passage.

word:hebrew:H4943.explanation: Mesheq means possession and can also refer to a steward. The passage uses it for the steward of a household.

word:hebrew:H507.explanation: Eleph is a proper name, rendered “Eleph” in English. It identifies a named location in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears only once, in Joshua 18:28. Because the available information preserves the name rather than giving an explicit definition, its meaning is best understood as the name itself, not as a translated description or common noun. Its precise significance in Joshua 18:28 depends on the surrounding passage and the list of locations in that chapter.

word:hebrew:H5074.explanation: Nâdad means to wander or flee. It can also mean to drive away.

word:hebrew:H5157.explanation: Nachal means to inherit. It can refer to inheriting land allotted by lot. In another use, it means causing others to inherit. It can also describe distributing an inheritance.

word:hebrew:H5272.explanation: This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Neiel.” It identifies a named place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Joshua 19:27. Because the available text gives no further lexical definition, its clearest meaning is the name itself: Neiel. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the place’s role in the territorial description.

word:hebrew:H5290.explanation: No'ar means boyhood, referring to childhood or youth.

word:hebrew:H5328.explanation: Nitstsah means a blossom or flower.

word:hebrew:H5351.explanation: Nequddah means a boss or stud.

word:hebrew:H5401.explanation: Nashaq means to kiss. It is used when family members kiss one another.

word:hebrew:H5478.explanation: Suwchah means something swept away, such as filth. It can also describe something torn.

word:hebrew:H5629.explanation: This Hebrew word means “remnant”: the part that remains after something has been used, removed, or separated. It functions as a noun, naming what is left rather than describing an action. In its only occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears in Exodus 26:12. The surrounding verse context is needed to see precisely what remains there and how that remaining portion relates to the surrounding instructions.

word:hebrew:H5665.explanation: Abed-Nego is a personal name used for one of the men appointed over the affairs of Babylon.

word:hebrew:H5760.explanation: ʻăvîyl means morally perverse, describing an ungodly person.

word:hebrew:H5782.explanation: Uw means to wake, literally or figuratively. It describes waking from sleep and can also describe stirring people or their spirits to action.

word:hebrew:H5827.explanation: Ezer is a personal name, referring to an individual in a genealogy. It functions as the name of a person rather than as a general description or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 7:21, within a family record. The available rendering preserves the name as “Ezer,” so its broader lexical meaning cannot be stated from this word’s recorded use alone. Its immediate role is to identify a particular person in the genealogy.

word:hebrew:H5885.explanation: This Hebrew word is a place-name, referring to Enshemesh, also rendered “Shemesh.” It identifies a location in the Old Testament, not an ordinary description or action. The name occurs four times in the Hebrew Bible, in two verses of Joshua: Joshua 15:7 and Joshua 18:17. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise significance as a location cannot be explained further; its supported meaning here is the geographical name itself.

word:hebrew:H5940.explanation: Ĕlîy means a pestle, used with a mortar to grind grain.

word:hebrew:H6008.explanation: Amad is a Hebrew name preserved as “Amad” in English Bible renderings. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 19:26. Because the available information identifies the word chiefly through its preserved name rather than an explicit definition, it is best understood as a specific designation, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word. Its precise role in Joshua 19:26 depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:hebrew:H6071.explanation: Asis means fresh grape juice and can also refer to new or sweet wine.

word:hebrew:H6219.explanation: Ashowth means shining or polished; in this context, it describes iron as bright.

word:hebrew:H6303.explanation: This Hebrew word is a personal name rendered “Padon.” It functions as a name rather than as a description, command, or action word. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Ezra 2:44 and once in Nehemiah 7:47. Because no lexical definition or surrounding verse text is available here, its meaning is best understood as the identity of the person named, not as a broader concept or theological term.

word:hebrew:H6376.explanation: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Pishon.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action, identifying a specific entity in the Old Testament. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, at Genesis 2:11, so its meaning is focused and does not represent a broad category of repeated uses. The precise significance of the named entity in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself is the name Pishon.

word:hebrew:H6493.explanation: This Hebrew word describes someone as “seeing,” referring to the ability to perceive or recognize what is before them. It occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Exodus. As a descriptive word, it characterizes a person rather than naming an action or object. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and how the description functions there.

word:hebrew:H6530.explanation: Periyts means violent. It can also describe a destroyer or robber.

word:hebrew:H6642.explanation: Tsâbaṭ means to grasp—that is, to reach out and hand something to another.

word:hebrew:H6707.explanation: Tsechichah means a parched region or dry land—a desert.

word:hebrew:H6826.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a covering or an overlaying—a layer placed over something else. It is used for the metal covering or plating associated with the tabernacle and sacred objects, and later for the overlaying connected with an image. Across its five Old Testament occurrences, the central idea remains something that covers, coats, or lies over another object. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is on the covering itself or the act of overlaying.

word:hebrew:H693.explanation: Orab means to lurk or lie in wait. It can also describe people lying in ambush against someone.

word:hebrew:H6934.explanation: Kadmiel is a personal name used for Israelites. It is listed among the Levites more than once.

word:hebrew:H6981.explanation: Kore is the name of two Israelites.

word:hebrew:H7043.explanation: Qalal means to be or make light. It can describe something becoming lessened, as when waters abated, or being treated with contempt, as when Sarai was despised. It is also used for cursing a person.

word:hebrew:H7115.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “anguish,” a state of severe inner distress. It describes a burden that can weigh heavily on a person and hinder a free response. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears only once, in Exodus 6:9. That single occurrence makes the surrounding verse especially important for understanding its particular force there, but the word’s basic sense remains anguish.

word:hebrew:H7252.explanation: Reba means lying down, especially for sleep.

word:hebrew:H7304.explanation: Ravach means to be refreshed or revived. It can also refer to having ample room.

word:hebrew:H7483.explanation: Raamah means the mane of a horse, pictured as quivering in the wind. In the same description, it is rendered as “thunder.”

word:hebrew:H7577.explanation: Rethuqah means something fastened, such as a chain.

word:hebrew:H7599.explanation: Shâ'an means to be at ease. It can also describe being quiet. It can also describe resting.

word:hebrew:H7609.explanation: “Sheerah” is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:24. Because the available wording functions as a name and the verse text is not provided here, the name itself does not establish additional meaning beyond identifying that person. Its significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding account.

word:hebrew:H7645.explanation: Shebaniah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Shebaniah.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs seven times, appearing once in 1 Chronicles and six times in Nehemiah. Several occurrences place Shebaniah among people involved in worship, public reading, or covenant-related activities, but the name itself does not describe those roles. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H7818.explanation: This Hebrew verb means “pressed.” It describes applying pressure to something, functioning as an action word rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 40:11, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its normal sense remains the action of pressing, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being pressed and how the action fits the sentence.

word:hebrew:H7986.explanation: Shalleṭeth means a vixen. It can also mean imperious, as in a description of a woman.

word:hebrew:H8033.explanation: Sham means there, pointing to a place. It can also mean then when it marks a time. It may also mean thence, marking movement from a place.

word:hebrew:H811.explanation: Eshkol means a bunch or cluster of grapes.

word:hebrew:H8262.explanation: Shaqats means to loathe or detest. It can also mean to make something abominable.

word:hebrew:H8280.explanation: Sârah means to prevail or to have power.

word:hebrew:H8367.explanation: Shathaq means to subside. It can describe a stormy sea becoming calm.

word:hebrew:H8437.explanation: Tolal means an oppressor—one who causes others to howl. It can describe those who waste and torment others.

word:hebrew:H8495.explanation: Tayish means a buck or male goat.

word:hebrew:H8631.explanation: Teqêph means to become strong. It can also mean to make something strong or firm.

word:hebrew:H8648.explanation: This Hebrew word means “two.” It is a numeral used to identify a quantity of two, whether counting people, objects, or occurrences. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times, so its basic meaning is consistent but relatively uncommon. Its role is straightforward: it tells the reader that the number involved is two. The surrounding sentence determines what is being counted, while the word itself supplies the number.

word:hebrew:H868.explanation: Ethnan means a gift, hire, or reward given as the price of prostitution.

word:hebrew:H932.explanation: Bohan is a proper name preserved in English as “Bohan,” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive meaning. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Joshua, and the two occurrences are found in Joshua 15:6 and Joshua 18:17. The available wording identifies how the name is rendered, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the specific referent in each passage.
